ReleaseTools provides the `rt` command-line tool for iOS and macOS application releases.

Think [Fastlane](https://fastlane.tools/), but much simpler (and consequently much less capable).

The main activities supported are:
- calculating a build number and injecting it whilst building or archiving
- exporting and uploading an archive to the App Store portal
- (or) notarising and building a Sparkle feed for an externally distributed macOS app.

## Uploading To App Store

When publishing via the App Store Connect portal, the main command is:

```shell
rt submit
```

This builds an archive, exports it, and uploads it to App Store Connect using the configured credentials.

### Granularity

The `submit` command is the equivalent of performing this sequence of smaller commands:

```shell
    rt archive
    rt export
    rt upload
```

The effect of these commands is:
- archive: build an archive
- export: export from output of `archive`
- upload: upload the output of `export` to the app store connect portal

Normally you can just use the `submit` command, but the individual steps
can also executed in order if you want more control over the process, or
if you need to restart the halfway through (eg run the export again
without rebuilding or exporting the archive).

Direct macOS distribution commands handle notarization, compression, Sparkle appcast generation, and website publishing.

# Build Number

ReleaseTools can automatically calculate and inject a build number into your application.

You can either do this only when making an archive for distribution (running `rt archive` or `rt submit`), or every time you make a build.

Generating metadata when archiving avoids an extra build step, but leaves that metadata unavailable during normal Xcode builds.

To generate metadata during normal builds, run `rt update-build` in a script phase.

## When Archiving

When archiving, the injected build number is based solely on the value of the git version tag attached to the current HEAD commit.

This version must be in the form `vX.Y.Z-BUILD` where `X.Y.Z` is the semantic version, and `BUILD` is the build number.

If there is not a tag in this format at HEAD, the `archive`/`submit` commands will refuse to run.

If the tag is present, then it is parsed and used to set the value of three constants:
- RT_BUILD: the calculated build number
- RT_COMMIT: the full git commit hash
- RT_VERSION: the semantic version string (e.g., "1.2.3")

The archive command then generates a `VersionInfo.h` header file, and overrides some build settings on the command line when invoking `xcodebuild`, so that the header file is included by the Info.plist preprocessor.

The build settings supplied to `xcodebuild` on the command line are:
- INFOPLIST_PREFIX_HEADER: set to the location of the generated `VersionInfo.h` file
- INFOPLIST_PREPROCESS: set to YES
- RT_BUILD: set to the calculated build number
- RT_COMMIT: the full git commit hash
- RT_VERSION: the semantic version string

By turning on the Info.plist preprocessing, and using our generated header file, we cause any occurences of the strings `RT_BUILD`, `RT_COMMIT`, and `RT_VERSION` in the Info.plist file to be replaced with the values of the corresponding constants.

By also defining the three variables directly as command line arguments when we invoke xcodebuild, we also allow any occurences of `${RT_BUILD}`, `${RT_COMMIT}`, and `${RT_VERSION}` to be replaced in other build settings or build scripts.

## When Building

The `update-build` command calculates build metadata without requiring a version tag at HEAD.

It uses the highest existing build number plus one, checking both platform-agnostic and platform-specific tags. The version comes from the tag with the highest build number, or defaults to `1.0.0` when no version tags exist.

Select a header output with `--header=<path>` or an Xcode build-settings output with `--config=<path>`. Both contain `RT_BUILD`, `RT_COMMIT`, and `RT_VERSION`. Include the generated file in your project.

For property-list output, supply `--plist=<source>` and `--plist-dest=<destination>`. When the calculated build differs from the source’s `CFBundleVersion`, the command writes the destination with updated `CFBundleVersion`, `Commit`, and `Version` values, plus an `RTInfo.h` header beside it.

## Incrementing The Build Number

ReleaseTools supports automatically incrementing the version tag, using the `rt tag` command.

This command creates a platform-agnostic `v<version>-<build>` tag at HEAD, using the highest existing build number plus one unless an explicit build is supplied. If HEAD already has a version tag, it reports the existing tag, for example: `A version tag already exists at HEAD: v1.0.0-267.`




# The Full Toolchain

The process of producing a release consists of a number of steps: archiving, exporting, notarizing, stapling, zipping, updating, regenerating an appcast, and publishing.

ReleaseTools is designed to be easy to debug when something goes wrong, and so each step is broken down into separate command. This makes it possible to re-run some steps without having to start at the beginning each time.

There are also `--show-commands` and `--show-output` options which will echo the commands that the tool is running, and the output of those commands.

When everything is working smoothly, however, the steps are expected to be run one after the other, without the need for interaction. A shell script to run them all together in the correct order, for a macOS release being distributed via an external website, might look something like:

```shell
set -e
rt archive --show-commands
rt export --distribution
rt notarize
rt wait
rt compress
rt appcast --show-commands
rt publish
```
## Commands

More details of each command are given below:

### archive

Run `xcodebuild archive` to archive the application for distribution.

Select the scheme with `--scheme` or the `defaults.scheme` configuration setting. Without either, `rt` uses the discovered workspace name.

The archive is placed into: `.build/<platform>/archive.xcarchive`.

### export

Exports `.build/<platform>/archive.xcarchive` into `.build/<platform>/export`. Use `--distribution` for Developer ID distribution; the default export method is App Store Connect.

### notarize

Compresses the exported application and submits it using `xcrun altool --notarize-app`.

If the upload succeeds, the Apple servers return an xml receipt containing a RequestUUID that we can use to check on the status later. This is stored in `.build/<platform>/export/receipt.xml`.

### upload

Uploads the exported `.pkg` for macOS or `.ipa` for other platforms to App Store Connect.

The upload response is saved to `.build/<platform>/upload/receipt.json`, and the tool's stderr is saved to `.build/<platform>/upload/errors.log`, including when the upload fails.

Rejections report Apple's error code and complete message. Recognized release-version and sandbox failures provide focused guidance. Unsupported-Xcode failures report `Xcode version <version> (<build>) not accepted by App Store Connect`, using `CFBundleShortVersionString` and `ProductBuildVersion` from the upload application's `Contents/version.plist`. The application is located using the receipt's `tool-path`. If its metadata is unavailable or incomplete, the error omits the version and build. The receipt's `tool-version` is the upload tool's version.

### wait

Polls the saved submission identifier using `xcrun altool --notarization-info`.

If the status is `success`, we copy the exported app from `.build/<platform>/export` into `.build/<platform>/stapled`, and staple it with the notarization ticket.

If the status is `invalid`, we abort with an error that includes Apple's status message and the issues listed in the notarization log.

If the status is not yet known (notarization hasn't completed), we wait 30 seconds and check again.

This command will therefore not return until notarization has completed (or failed).

### compress

Compresses the app in `.build/<platform>/stapled` into a zip archive suitable for inclusion in the `appcast`.

The versioned archive is named `<app>-v<version>-<build>.zip` and written to the directory selected with `--updates=<path>`.

A copy named `<app>-latest.zip` is placed in the website directory selected with `--website=<path>`.

The default locations are `Dependencies/Website/updates` for versioned archives and `Dependencies/Website` for the latest archive.

### appcast

Rebuilds the appcast file, using Sparkle's `generate_appcast` command, which it builds first if necessary.

The feed is generated in the updates directory selected with `--updates=<path>`.

The default updates directory is `Dependencies/Website/updates`.

The appcast generator uses a private DSA key from the selected keychain, named `<workspace> Sparkle Key`.

The key-generation flow uses Sparkle’s `generate_keys` script and imports the private key into the keychain. When the command requests a key rename, use Keychain Access to rename `Imported Private Key` to the name shown in the error, then rerun the command.

The public key is expected to be called `dsa_pub.pem`, and be included in the `Resources/` folder of the app bundle.

In order to be able to build/run the various Sparkle tools, the Sparkle project is expected to be present in the Xcode workspace.

Use `--show-output` to display subprocess output while working with signing tools and the keychain.

### publish

Commits tracked changes in the website repository and pushes them to its remote. Select the repository with `--website=<path>`; its default location is `Dependencies/Website`. The updates directory is selected with `--updates=<path>`.

### update-build

This command can be used to inject the current build number
and commit hash into a C-style header file,
an xcconfig file, or an Info.plist file.

If you specify the `--header` option with a path to a `.h` file, it
will be replaced with generated content:

```c
#define RT_BUILD <build>
#define RT_COMMIT <hash>
#define RT_VERSION <version>
```

containing the current build number, commit hash, and version string values.

If you specify the `--config` option with a path to an `.xcconfig` file, it will be generated with the same values as above.

Use `--plist=<source>` and `--plist-dest=<destination>` to write updated `CFBundleVersion`, `Commit`, and `Version` metadata when the source build number differs. This also writes `RTInfo.h` beside the destination.

### submit

This performs the `archive`, `export` and `upload` commands in order.

It accepts the same options as those commands.

## Building

Build the tool with Swift Package Manager: `swift build`.

You can build and run in a single line with `swift run rt <command> <args>`.

Alternatively you can build & install it somewhere, eg using [Mint](https://github.com/yonaskolb/Mint).

ReleaseTools is distributed as the `rt` executable. Run it directly or from a shell build phase.

# Configuration

To cut down on the amount of configuration that you have to do, `rt` relies on naming conventions and defaults for a lot of things.

Run `rt` from the project root. Set the workspace with `--workspace`, or let `rt` discover an `.xcworkspace` at that root. The default scheme is the configured `defaults.scheme`, falling back to the discovered workspace name.

You can override the default scheme with the `--scheme=<name>` option, or with a setting in the optional `.rt/config.json` configuration file.

Project configuration lives in a `.rt/` directory. The base committed configuration goes in `.rt/config.json`, and git-ignored local overrides go in `.rt/local/config.json`.

Optional platform and scheme overrides are loaded from:

- `.rt/platforms/<platform>.json`
- `.rt/schemes/<scheme>.json`
- `.rt/schemes/<scheme>/platforms/<platform>.json`
- matching git-ignored overrides under `.rt/local/...`

The same layout is supported for global defaults under `$XDG_CONFIG_HOME/rt/` when `XDG_CONFIG_HOME` is set, or `~/.local/config/rt/` otherwise.

Each config file uses the same schema:

```json
{
  "defaults": {
    "scheme": "Foo"
  },
  "settings": {
    "keychain": "~/Library/Keychains/login.keychain",
    "apiKey": "key-here",
    "apiIssuer": "issuer-here"
  }
}
```

Add `.rt/local/` to your repository’s `.gitignore` to keep private overrides out of source control.

We support building for multiple platforms, but only one at a time. To tell rt which platform to build for, use an optional argument `--platform=macOS|iOS|tvOS|watchOS`. If you don't supply the platform, it defaults to `macOS`.
